title: How Southern Hills Appliance Repair handles the 9 p.m. broken washer call
summary: Southern Hills Appliance Repair uses a call flow and Sona to sort every call, send leaks to the owner, and send booking requests to Jobber.
body_markdown:
It’s 9 p.m., a tenant’s washer has quit, and the phone is ringing at Southern Hills Appliance Repair. Carl Jarvis is at home, and his techs have gone for the day.


Before Sona,[Quo’s AI agent](http://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/overview) , that call would have gone to voicemail, and someone would have spent the next day chasing it. Now the tenant presses 2, and Sona picks up. It asks what any good dispatcher would ask: name, number, address, what’s broken, how urgent. Sona acknowledges that a broken washer is a real problem, then texts a link to Carl’s request form, which feeds straight into[Jobber](http://support.quo.com/core-concepts/integrations/jobber) . By morning, the call is waiting in Quo with the details filled in.


Carl owns Southern Hills, which covers a large stretch of Southern Alberta, and service calls often keep him and his techs out of the office. A phone system “that can manage things on its own, without me having to babysit all the way along,” he said, is “pretty critical to our operation.”


Carl’s setup starts with a call flow that decides where every call goes. From there, he trained Sona on appliance repair, then added a twice-daily brief that flags schedule conflicts before a technician heads out.


##


**1. Give every call a destination**


Every call starts the same way, with Quo checking[whether the office is open](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/business-hours) . During the day, callers hear a[short menu](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/phone-menu) ; if they don’t press anything, the call rings Carl’s office admin, and if the admin doesn’t pick up, it goes to Sona. After hours, callers are provided a choice: press 1 for voicemail or 2 to talk with Sona. However they get there, every branch ends somewhere: with a person, with Sona, or to voicemail.


Carl sorts each call with two questions. Is the caller a property manager or a homeowner? Does the problem need help now, or can it be booked for later?


The daytime menu has a hidden option: press 1 to reach Carl himself. The greeting doesn’t mention it, and that’s deliberate. “I don’t actually want to be the first line of communication,” he said. Callers who don’t press anything get sent to his office admin, then to Sona, so only people who already know the shortcut get through to him. He’s now considering a separate branch for certain callers, so they can reach him directly while everyone else still goes through the admin or Sona.


The whole arrangement is easy to change. With his previous phone provider, rerouting a number meant emailing or calling the company; now Carl can do it himself in about five minutes, with a few clicks in the[call flow builder](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/overview) . He built the original call flow himself by dragging a few boxes around, then made a couple of rounds of tweaks to get the routing and the greeting right.


### How to route calls by business hour in Quo


**


1. Go to **Settings** → **Phone numbers** , select your number, turn on **Enable business hours** , and set your time zone and schedule.
2. Click **Edit call flow** and drag a **Business hours** step after the **Incoming call** trigger, so daytime and after-hours calls take different routes.
3. On the **During hours** path, add a **Phone menu** step. Click **Add greeting message** and write the greeting as[text-to-speech](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/guides/text-to-speech-guide) , record it, or upload an audio file (MP3 or WAV), then click **Add keypad option** for each choice the greeting lists.
4. For callers who press nothing, set the no selection path to a **Ring users** step for your office person. Below it, add a[Go to](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/go-to-step) step that sends unanswered calls to your Sona step, so you can reuse one Sona instead of building two. **Go to** can only point at a step that already exists, so add your Sona step first (see section 2).
5. For after hours, add a second **Phone menu** : 1 for voicemail, 2 for Sona. Note that you don’t have to provide a choice at all: you can simply send every after hours call to Sona or voicemail (or even forward callers to a different phone number entirely) if you prefer.
6. To draft changes without touching your live setup, click[+ Create new call flow](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/temp-call-flows) and build it there. Publishing replaces your live flow. Publish it when you’re ready.


**Note:** Phone menus are available on Business and Scale plans.


*You can schedule a different call flow ahead of time for holidays. Click the arrow next to* ***Publish now*** *, choose*[Schedule](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/administration/call-flows/temp-call-flows) *to publish later, and pick a date and time. Then schedule your regular flow to resume afterward, or the holiday one will keep running.*


##


**2. Teach Sona your trade, then give it jobs**


Carl uses Sona during the day as well as after hours, and for good reason. Appliance repair, he said, is “notorious for people calling in and monopolizing your time.” Callers want a diagnosis over the phone, which isn’t how his business works. “I’m happy to talk to people,” he said, “but I want to give them pertinent information.”


So he loaded Sona’s[knowledge](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/knowledge) with a database of error codes. When a caller specifically reads out an E6 on their dishwasher, Sona checks it against the database for that model, explains that it’s most likely a leak error, and tells them someone should come out to fix it right away. A booking link follows by text.


To Carl, Sona “sounds like how we would do an intake.” He added a line telling callers that, yes, Sona is AI, but that a human reviews every call. That caveat, he said, was one of the changes that made a bigger difference in callers following through with Sona.


The payoff arrives the next morning, when Carl opens Quo and finds the washer call complete, with its structure already built. Voicemail never worked that well for him. “People just assume no one’s going to check them anyways,” he said. Now, “I don’t have to listen to the voicemail three times to try to catch the phone number.”


### How to set up Sona to triage calls in Quo


**


1. Open the Sona step, click **Personality** , and set its voice and tone.
2. Write a[greeting](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/overview) that names your business, tells callers they’re speaking to AI, says the call is recorded, and that a person reviews every call. Only say a person reviews calls if one does. You can use this example, and swap in the name of your company: “Hi, you’ve reached Southern Hills Appliance Repair. I’m an AI agent, and someone on our team reviews every call, so tell me what’s going on and I’ll make sure it gets handled. This call is being recorded.”
3. **Add knowledge** . Import your website, upload a file such as a PDF or CSV (up to 10 MB), or write a page in Sona. Troubleshooting information like error codes goes in knowledge. Instructions for what Sona should do, like sending a link, go in jobs. Keep one topic per page (a page holds up to 20,000 characters), for example one page per brand. Toggle the page on in your Sona step, then publish the call flow. Page edits apply right away, but attachment changes only go live when you publish.
4. Add trade terms and brand names to **Vocabulary** (in the Sona step, open **Knowledge** , then select **Vocabulary** ) so Sona recognizes them. You can add up to 25 words, and they apply across your whole workspace.
5. Click **Test Sona** and place a mock call, reading out an error code, before you publish.


*Callout:* ***Knowledge*** *pages can’t hold clickable links, so describe locations in plain text and put the booking link in a job. Write each fact so it stands on its own.*

### **Escalate urgent calls, and book the rest**


Carl set up an[escalation job](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/jobs-configuration) so that water leaks and deep freezes get transferred to him. He wrote the rules the way he’d brief an office admin: “Hey, if this happens, do this.” Then, he used Optimize to turn them into structured conditions. “It’s very robust in the way that it can handle different scenarios,” he said, “which I was very impressed with.”


For callers who just want to book, a[scheduling job](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/sona-job-guide) texts them a link to his request form and confirms it arrived. The form feeds into Jobber as an unscheduled visit, a step Carl used to handle by hand before he automated it. The caller, meanwhile, “can actually go to bed knowing that their problem is being handled.” As Carl put it, “nobody thinks their appliances are important until they don’t work.”


### How to send urgent calls to the owner and text a booking link in Quo


**


1. In the Sona step, click **Add job** to create an escalation job. Describe when Sona should transfer the call in plain language, then type / and choose[Transfer call](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/actions) . For example: “If the caller reports water leaking or a freezer that has stopped working, transfer the call to Carl.” Choose who gets the call: a workspace member, a shared inbox, or an external number outside Quo. Sona confirms with the caller, then leaves the call. If the person doesn’t answer, the caller reaches their voicemail, so pick someone reliable.
2. Add a scheduling job. List what Sona should collect (name, appliance, problem, how urgent) and write the text it sends with your booking or request-form link. Type / and choose[Send SMS](https://support.quo.com/core-concepts/ai-automations/sona/actions) to add it. Add opt-out language, such as “Reply STOP to opt out.” **Send SMS** needs a number registered for business messaging ([A2P 10DLC](https://support.quo.com/getting-started/carrier-registration/carrier-registration) or toll-free).
3. Click **Optimize** to rewrite your instructions in a format Sona handles well, then read them back. Click Undo if you prefer your original. Attach the job to your Sona step (up to 10 per step), click **Test Sona** , and publish the call flow.
4. If you use Jobber, go to **Settings** → **Integrations** → **Jobber** and connect your account. Quo then creates a Jobber request for new callers and syncs call summaries and transcripts. To have Sona create a request during the call, type /Create request in the scheduling job. You need Owner or Admin permissions, and Transcribe and summarize calls turned on for your number.


**Note:** The Jobber integration is available on Business and Scale plans.


##


**3. Start and end the day with a brief**


Once the calls are handled, Carl turns to AI to save time on scheduling and follow-up. Quo connects directly to[Claude](https://www.quo.com/integrations/claude) and[ChatGPT](https://www.quo.com/integrations/chatgpt) so that the AI can see his calls and texts. Every morning and evening, it writes him a brief that checks the day’s Jobber schedule against Quo, Gmail, and Google Calendar for anything that could cause a delay. “It just pulls all these different layers and brings them into one spot,” Carl said.


The brief also catches scheduling conflicts before they cost his team a trip. Say a customer replies the night before to say they can’t make it, but their appointment is still booked for first thing. The brief flags the mismatch, and Carl sorts it out before a technician heads out.


The same AI drafts replies to customers. When someone asks when their visit is, it checks Jobber and comes back with a proposed text for Carl to review: “According to your CRM, it says Tuesday at three. Is that still accurate? Do you want me to send this?” Carl just has to click accept, and the message goes out through Quo.


### How to set up a morning and evening brief with Quo and AI


**


1. Connect Quo to[Claude](https://www.quo.com/integrations/claude) or[ChatGPT](https://www.quo.com/integrations/chatgpt) .
2. Connect any other tools your brief should read, such as your field service software ([Jobber](https://www.quo.com/integrations/jobber) , in Carl’s case), email, and calendar.
3. Ask for the brief in plain language. For example: “Each evening and morning, list the day’s jobs from Jobber, check them against new calls and texts in Quo, my email, and my calendar, and flag anything that could hold up a technician, like a customer who says they can’t make it.”
4. Create it as a[scheduled task in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10291617-scheduled-tasks-in-chatgpt) or a[recurring task with Claude](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-scheduled-tasks) .
5. To handle replies, ask the AI to draft each text from your field service software and wait for your approval before sending it through Quo.


##


**Start with the call flow**


The tenant’s washer call is waiting for Carl the next morning, with details in Quo, the request in Jobber, and a brief that’s already checked the appointment against the day’s schedule. “It all starts with a clean call flow and setting up Sona for as much as you can,” Carl said.
